# Your Toolkit

This part asks what you work with every day, how you keep a
history of that work, and how you make it run on another machine.
It belongs to the first quarter, and every later chapter assumes
it. That is, the editor, the version history, and the project
environment set up here are used without further explanation from
Part III onward.

- @sec-shell teaches the Unix shell: moving around the filesystem,
  inspecting a raw file before R reads it, and composing pipelines.
  It is optional. Later chapters give the few commands they need
  in full, and a reader who has used a terminal can skip it.
- @sec-workstation installs R, an IDE, Quarto, and Git, and verifies
  the machine with a checklist.
- @sec-git-solo introduces Git and GitHub for a single analyst who
  wants a recoverable history.
- @sec-git-teams extends that history to a team: branches, pull
  requests, review, and conflicts.
- @sec-renv records the package versions an analysis uses in a
  lockfile and restores them elsewhere.
- @sec-docker pins the R version, operating system, and system
  libraries in a container.
- @sec-zzcollab assembles Git, `renv`, and Docker into a research
  compendium and audits it against the Five Pillars.
- @sec-ai-coding sets out how to prompt language models and coding
  agents, how to check what they produce, and what may be sent to
  them. It comes before the chapters in which you rely on them.

If the quiz at the start of a chapter is easy, skip to the next.
The three environment chapters each add one layer and are best
read in order. A reader who already uses Git daily may move
quickly through @sec-git-solo, but should still read
@sec-ai-governance before sending any project file to a model.
